title: Eating well on a student budget
description: Good food on little money is a skill, not a sacrifice: a few staples, a short list of reliable meals, and a freezer doing quiet work.

body.heading: Build around cheap staples
paragraphs: Rice, pasta, oats, lentils, eggs, frozen vegetables, and tinned tomatoes are inexpensive in almost every shop and combine into dozens of meals. A store cupboard stocked with staples means dinner is always mostly bought already.
Lentils and beans deserve special mention: they cost little, need no soaking in their tinned form, keep for ages, and turn a thin soup or sauce into a meal that actually fills you.

body.heading: Cook once, eat twice
paragraphs: Cooking for one is the most expensive way to eat. Cook double and freeze the second portion, and future tired-you gets a free, instant meal on the evening when takeaway would otherwise win.
A small rotation of meals you can cook without thinking — a curry, a pasta sauce, a stir-fry, a soup — beats a shelf of recipe books. Skill with five meals feeds you better than ambition about fifty.

body.heading: Shop with a plan and a time limit
paragraphs: Shop from a list, after eating if you can manage it, and compare unit prices on your staples. Supermarket own-brand versions of basic ingredients are usually indistinguishable in a cooked dish, and the difference across a term is real money.

Reduced-price shelves near closing time are worth learning, too: bread, fruit, and ready items are often marked down heavily. Freeze what you can, plan tomorrow's meal around the rest, and the savings repeat weekly.

takeaway: Stock cheap staples, cook double and freeze the extra, and master five reliable meals — eating well at student prices is a system, not a struggle.
